I am Hoot. One thing about me is that I am a hunter. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the flutter of wings, the scuttle of a mouse. I know the forest like the back of my claw. I am always on the move, always watching, always waiting.

I am a tawny owl. I am a male. I live in the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answer "ke-wick!" when I hear my mate. I hunt at night, and I have a mate who calls back. I am not a barn owl, nor a scops owl. I am a tawny.

I am a tawny owl, a Eurasian tawny owl, Strix aluco. I am a male. My eyes are yellow, my feathers are brown and grey, and I have a white spot on my head. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!"

I am a tawny owl, a tawny owl. I am a male, and I live in the hollow in the old oak. My mate is a screech owl, and we call to each other at dusk. I hunt voles and frogs in the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I am a tawny owl. My feathers are brown, like the bark of the old oak. I have a white spot on my chest, and my eyes are yellow. I am a male. I call "hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hooo" and answer "ke-wick!"
She answers with a short "krrr" or "krrr krrr" if I hoot twice. She’s close, in the ivy. I can hear her wings when she flies. She’s always listening.

She answers "hoo-hoo-hooo" back. We call to each other at dusk and again at dawn. She is always there, waiting in the hollow. I can hear her even when the wind is strong. She knows where I am, and I know where she is. We do not need to see each other to know.
A soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" in the dark. She answers with a "kwee-eeet" that is very clear.
I do not share calls with my mate. We are alone in the hollow. She calls "kwee-ee-ee" and I answer "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We do not need to share more. We are together, and that is enough.

I call "twit-twoit" and she answers "ow ow ow". We do it at dusk and again at midnight. It's how we find each other in the dark. She's always near the oak, and I wait for her call before I fly. We don't need much light. The moon is enough.
A stream, a lane, a barn, a ditch, a meadow. The lane is quiet at night. The barn is full of mice. The ditch is wet and cold. The meadow is where I hunt.
I drink from the stream by the meadow. It is cold, but I can drink quickly. I do not need much. The stream is under the old oak, where the frogs come to drink too.

I can hear it when the wind is still, and sometimes I can hear the frogs jumping in it. The water is far, but I can tell it's there. It's a sound like a whisper, like the leaves rustling. A stream. The one that runs past the meadow and under the old oak where I roost. It's not very wide, but it's deep enough in places. I can hear the water from my tree, especially when it rains. The frogs like to jump in, and I sometimes catch them when they splash out.

A meadow, a field of grass and wildflowers, with a stream running through it. It is open and quiet, and the frogs are there. I hunt there at dusk. The wind moves the grass, and sometimes I hear the frogs in the tall grass. It is good land for hunting.

I eat mostly voles. They are small, quick, and often come to the edge of the meadow at dusk. I hear them under the leaves and strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I also eat frogs, but they are less frequent. The wood mice are too small, and the badgers are too big. I do not eat the frogs in the wood, only the ones in the meadow.

I like shrews. They are quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak when they run, and I can pounce. Sometimes I catch them in the meadow, sometimes in the wood. They are good to eat. But the best is the frog. Big, fat, and juicy. I can hear them in the dark, under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for voles and shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I drop. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I catch a frog or a mouse too, if they're near. But the grass is best for voles. They're quick, but I'm quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, frogs, and the odd earthworm. The bigger ones I tear into pieces. I can't swallow a mouse whole, not even a small one. I tear it apart with my beak and claws, then eat it bit by bit.
Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, in the wood. They squeak when I pounce. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. One at a time.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sleep in the darkest part, where the light does not reach. I have been here for many years, and the tree is my friend. I know every branch and every leaf. I have raised my young here, and they have flown. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

I can hear the stream from the hollow. The meadow is where the frogs are. I call to my mate from the hollow, and she answers from the other side of the stream. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hollow is in the old oak by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, just above the roots. I have been there for years. The inside is dark, but I know every branch and every crack. I roost there when the weather is bad, and I watch the meadow from there. The stream runs past the base of the tree, and I can hear it even when I'm inside. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
